Okay, so I'm trying to figure out which geologic process caused the formation of Mount St. Helens. The options are converging boundaries, diverging boundaries, transform faults, or rift zones. From what I remember, Mount St. Helens is part of the Cascade Range, which is known for its volcanic activity. I think the Cascade Range is located along the west coast of the United States, in the Pacific Northwest.

I've heard that the Cascade Range is a result of tectonic activity, specifically subduction. Subduction is when one plate dives under another, right? So, maybe the Juan de Fuca Plate is subducting beneath the North American Plate. That would make sense because the Juan de Fuca Plate is an oceanic plate, and the North American Plate is a continental plate. Oceanic plates are denser, so when they subduct, they cause the continental plate to rise, leading to volcanic activity.

Looking at the options, converging boundaries involve the collision of two plates, which is exactly what's happening here. Diverging boundaries are more associated with mid-ocean ridges, where new crust is created. Transform faults are horizontal movements, like the San Andreas Fault in California, which doesn't seem related. Rift zones are associated with extension, like the East African Rift, which also doesn't fit here.

So, putting it all together, the formation of Mount St. Helens is due to the converging boundaries where the Juan de Fuca Plate subducts beneath the North American Plate. That points to option A as the correct answer.
